title: Learnings from LKMP: How to contribute to the Linux Kernel
text: Kernel developers have a reputation for being hard on newcomers. My experience was the opposite. Over the LFX Linux Kernel Bug Fixing Mentorship with Shuah Khan, nine of my patches were applied upstream: eight in the Industrial I/O (IIO) subsystem and one in the sfc network driver. None of them reached that state as I first wrote them. Each was improved by someone on the mailing list: a maintainer, a reviewer, or an automated test robot. This post is an account of that collaboration as much as of the bugs themselves.

title: Learnings from LKMP: How to contribute to the Linux Kernel
text:
Background: how a patch travels
The Linux kernel has no pull requests. A change is a plain-text email, sent with git send-email to the maintainers and lists that scripts/get_maintainer.pl names for the files it touches. Reviewers reply inline, and they show approval with tags such as Reviewed-by: and Acked-by:. A subsystem maintainer then applies the patch to their own tree. From there it flows into linux-next, then into Linus Torvalds’ mainline tree during a merge window, and, if it is marked for stable, into the stable kernels people already run.






flowchart LR
    A[Prepare<br/>and check] --> B[Send to<br/>the list]
    B --> C{Review}
    C -- v2 --> C
    C -- tags --> D[Maintainer<br/>tree]
    D --> E[linux-next]
    E --> F[Mainline]
    D -. stable .-> G[Stable<br/>kernels]




Figure 1: The path every patch in this post followed. Preparing means building with W=1 and running checkpatch and kernel-doc; the review loop is where most of the work happened.





IIO, maintained by Jonathan Cameron in iio.git, has two main branches. Fixes go to fixes-togreg and reach mainline in the current release cycle. Everything else goes to togreg, through a testing branch, and waits for the next merge window. This distinction matters later in the story.

title: Learnings from LKMP: How to contribute to the Linux Kernel
section: Learning the process the hard way
text:
Learning the process the hard way
My first attempt, in June 2025, did not reach any maintainer: I sent it as an attachment, only to my mentor. A second round, in June 2026, targeted the sm750fb staging driver. I had based it on an old tree, so I was renaming variables that other contributors had already renamed. The kernel test robot reported build failures, and my duplicate resubmissions earned a polite request to stop.
These were useful failures. They set the method I used for every later patch:

Start from today’s linux-next or the subsystem tree, never a stale checkout.
Build each changed object with make W=1, run scripts/checkpatch.pl --strict, and, for documentation, scripts/kernel-doc -Wall over the whole driver.
Search the list archives first. I kept local git mirrors of the linux-iio and netdev archives from lore.kernel.org, so I could check whether someone was already working on the same code.
Send each version once, with a changelog under the --- line.

title: Learnings from LKMP: How to contribute to the Linux Kernel
Learnings from LKMP: How to contribute to the Linux Kernel
section: Documentation, and why reviewers ask for more
text:
Documentation, and why reviewers ask for more
The remaining patches fixed kernel-doc comments that no longer matched the code: members that had been renamed or removed in ad5686, inv_icm42600, inv_mpu6050, and sfc. These sound minor, but the review of these patches taught me the most about how maintainers think.
When I sent a one-line fix for a stale @vdd_supply comment in inv_icm42600, Andy gave it a Reviewed-by: and asked whether it was the only kernel-doc problem in the driver. It was not. My v2 became a two-patch series that left the driver clean under kernel-doc -Wall. From then on I checked the whole driver before sending any documentation patch, and the inv_mpu6050 patch fixed all 13 of its warnings at once.
On netdev, Simon Horman noticed that a member next to the ones I had fixed in sfc was also undocumented. Looking closer, it was not used anywhere, so v2 removed it and two other unused members. That patch got Reviewed-by: tags from Alex Austin at AMD and from Simon, and Paolo Abeni applied it to net-next (lore, commit). It was my first patch applied anywhere in the kernel.

title: Learnings from LKMP: How to contribute to the Linux Kernel
text:
Working with the maintainers
I was nervous before every early submission. The names on the To: line were names I knew from MAINTAINERS files and commit logs, and every reply would be public and archived. That nervousness faded as the replies came in, because they were generous and precise.
Jonathan made me feel welcome from the start. When Jean-Baptiste called the startup-time fix “another good catch”, Jonathan replied “Absolutely” and applied it. He then suggested a follow-up, using named initialisers for the neighbouring .temp field, and added “No problem if you have moved onto other things!” It was a small sentence, but it made me feel like a contributor rather than a student.
He was also careful in ways that taught me about stewardship. On the cros_ec_sensors patch he wrote that the driver “tends to be well maintained”, so he would wait for its own maintainers before applying it. Tzung-Bi Shih, a ChromeOS EC maintainer, reviewed it the next morning, and Jonathan applied it that evening. When Joshua Crofts asked me for a Fixes: tag on that patch, I traced the code back to the commit that introduced it and posted the tag in the thread. Andy replied that there was no need to resend, because b4 collects tags from the whole thread. These are small things, but each of them is part of how the community works.
The best moment was a run of emails late on 17 October. Within about twenty minutes, “Applied to the togreg branch of iio.git” and “Applied to the fixes-togreg branch” arrived for seven of my patches. I was thrilled. After the earlier failures, seeing them applied one after another was the high point of the mentorship.

title: Learnings from LKMP: How to contribute to the Linux Kernel
text:
A lesson in dependencies
The follow-up Jonathan suggested taught me one more thing. I based it on fixes-togreg, because it edits lines that the startup-time fix had just changed. Joshua tried it on the development branch and replied that it did not apply. The patch was fine, but its context lines only exist where the startup-time fix exists. I explained this on the list. The lesson is to always state a patch’s base branch and dependencies below the --- line, especially when it builds on a fix that has not yet reached the development branch.

title: Learnings from LKMP: How to contribute to the Linux Kernel
text:
On using an AI assistant
I used an LLM-based assistant for analysis and to check my reasoning, and I disclosed it with an Assisted-by: tag on each patch, as the kernel’s policy on coding assistants requires. That policy is clear that responsibility stays with the human: I signed off, built and tested every patch, and answered every review myself. The guidance on the tag’s format changed during the mentorship. Andy corrected my early format, and Jonathan later dropped the tag from one patch because the guidance had changed again. It is a policy still being worked out, and the community is working it out in public.

title: Learnings from LKMP: How to contribute to the Linux Kernel
text:
For the next mentee

Read submitting-patches.rst before your first patch, and the subsystem’s maintainer notes, such as maintainer-netdev.rst, before your first patch to that subsystem.
Look for code that is wrong, not only code that warns. Tracing a bug to the commit that introduced it, with a Fixes: tag, makes a patch much more useful to maintainers.
When a reviewer asks for more than you sent, they are usually right. Treat it as the start of a collaboration.
Be patient. Maintainers batch their work, and my patches waited one to two weeks.

title: Why We Use Julia, 10 Years Later
text:
Ten years after the original “Why We Created Julia” post, the Julia blog asked its community to write back. About a hundred people did, each with a short, signed note. Most of them start the same way: someone tired of prototyping in Python or MATLAB and then rewriting the slow parts in C, who tried Julia out of curiosity and never left. There is an R job that went from eighteen hours to five minutes, and code running on aircraft collision-avoidance systems and lunar missions.
What I liked most is how often the story turns on a first pull request. Someone fixes a small thing, gets a careful review or a thumbs-up from a core developer, and a few years later is the one reviewing. That matched my own start in the Julia world, through JuliaSmoothOptimizers, TagBot and Qiskit.jl, closely enough that reading it felt a little like reading about people I already knew.
Why We Use Julia, 10 Years Later, The Julia Blog.

title: Quantum entanglement: A modern perspective
text:
This first appeared in Physics Today in April 2003, and the magazine brought it back in its archive series. I read it while starting my work on entanglement purification, and it was the first time the subject felt like one story rather than a list of results. It goes from Schrödinger’s cat and Bell’s inequalities to the modern view, where entanglement is a resource you can count, spend and move around.
The part I keep coming back to is the difference between how many perfect pairs it costs to make a noisy state and how many you can distill back out of it. For mixed states the second can be smaller, and for some states it is zero even though they are entangled, which the authors call the black holes of quantum information. Much of what I now work on, from purification protocols to scheduling in quantum networks, sits in that gap.
Quantum entanglement: A modern perspective, Physics Today.

title: An Illustrated Guide to Automatic Sparse Differentiation
text:
I found this while working on JuliaSmoothOptimizers, where every solver quietly asks for a sparse Jacobian or Hessian and I had never really asked how it gets one. One of the authors, Alexis Montoison, works in the same ecosystem, and the post reads like someone patiently answering that exact question. It starts from the chain rule, and the figure of a small convolution’s Jacobian, almost entirely empty, made the problem obvious before any equation did.
The idea that stayed with me is that two columns which never share a nonzero row can be computed together in one pass, and then pulled apart again. Finding which columns can share turns into a graph-coloring problem, and the Hessian version borrows its tricks from Powell, Toint, Coleman and Moré in the 1970s and 80s, long before machine learning cared. The authors are also careful to say when none of this pays off, which I appreciated more than the speedups.
An Illustrated Guide to Automatic Sparse Differentiation, ICLR 2025 Blogposts.

title: World Age for beginners
text:
For a long time “world age” was, to me, just the name of an error I got when I used eval inside a function and then tried to call what I had defined. The manual calls it an advanced topic most people never need, so I never looked further. This Discourse post changed that. It starts from a simpler question, why dynamic languages are usually slow, and only names world age once you already understand the problem it solves.
The point is that a compiler can only optimize what it can assume. Julia lets you redefine almost anything, so it promises one thing in return: a running call keeps seeing the world as it was when it started, and new definitions show up on the next call. That single rule lets Julia compile and cache code ahead of each call, and it explains why invokelatest exists. If you want the formal version, the post points to Belyakova et al. (OOPSLA 2020).
World Age for beginners: one way to compile a dynamic language, Julia Discourse.

title: Arnav Kapoor
text:
I am a fourth-year Computer Science major at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Bhopal. I work on the problem of making entanglement reliable enough to build real quantum networks, and on the broader question of how mathematical structure should guide algorithm design.
I am currently a Summer Research Intern at UMass Amherst with the Centre for Quantum Networks, advised by Dr. Filip Rozpedek and Dr. Stefan Krastanov. There I implement quantum convolutional codes, entanglement purification protocols, and quantum repeater simulations under realistic hardware noise in QuantumClifford.jl and QuantumSavory.jl.
In parallel, I am a research intern with Prof. Dominique Orban’s group at Polytechnique Montréal (JuliaSmoothOptimizers), translating classical smooth and non-smooth optimization problems into structured Julia formulations (JuMP, ADNLPModels) for OptimizationProblems.jl.

title: Software
text:
NCL.jl
A pure-Julia implementation of Algorithm NCL (Ma, Judd, Orban and Saunders) for nonlinearly constrained optimization, part of the JuliaSmoothOptimizers ecosystem. NCL is a stabilized augmented-Lagrangian method that solves a short sequence of subproblems regularized by residual variables, which keeps it reliable on problems that violate the LICQ. Its subproblems are solved by interior-point methods such as IPOPT, Artelys Knitro and MadNLP. I made the solver integrations optional package extensions, added support for maximization problems and Julia LTS, made NCL declare infeasibility at the maximum penalty, and tuned how barrier parameters are passed to MadNLP and Knitro.

title: Software
text:
Qiskit.jl
Julia bindings for Qiskit through its C API. I added a TranspileOptions wrapper, add_instruction and add_property on Target, a delay method on QuantumCircuit with Unitful.jl units, readable show methods for wrapped C objects, and minimum-version testing of dependencies, and fixed memory cleanup in count_ops.

title: Software
text:
TagBot
The GitHub Action that creates tags, releases and changelogs for Julia packages when they are registered, used across the Julia ecosystem. I have had over 20 pull requests merged, including changelog support for backport and yanked releases, a changelog_format option, correct handling of Registrator branches and subdirectory packages, case-insensitive registry lookups, and clearer error handling for rate limits, permissions and malformed TOML.

title: Software
text:
QiOpt4QNet-Simulator
A quantum-network simulation and optimization framework. It models repeater networks with limited quantum memory and noisy links, builds candidate route and purification bundles for service requests, and compares exact MILP, QUBO and quantum annealing, tensor-network and classical heuristic solvers for admitting them. I am the top contributor: I added the Metropolis annealer and tensor-network optimizer, a conflict-aware purification scheduler, joint scheduling, adaptive-QUBO and GNN extensions, and the CI setup.
